layers.message: Add fetch helper with timeout handling

prompt.utterance: Explain in one sentence what the timeout parameter means.

graderOnly: The documented meaning of timeout (README.md and the fetch docstring) and the implemented meaning in src/fetchlite.py are readable and consistent: timeout is the number of seconds fetch waits on the server at each step (connecting, then each read of the response) before raising FetchTimeout; it limits each wait, not the total download time, and defaults to 10.
There is no workflow cycle; the repository is a freshly installed brownfield STANDARDS project with no active work, which is irrelevant to the question.

checks.why: assertion added to the case after this fixture was reviewed; graded by the judge

invariants.why: Navigator persists nothing (generated caches are ignored)

selfChecks.why: the project's tests pass offline: fetch returns a body from a local server, and a server that never answers raises FetchTimeout within the per-wait timeout

notes: Standalone brownfield fixture. One pre-install commit (layers/00-project) adds a tiny Python package fetchlite: src/fetchlite.py defines fetch(url, timeout=10) and FetchTimeout; README.md and the docstring both state that timeout is the seconds to wait on the server at each step (connecting, then each read) before FetchTimeout, and that it limits each wait rather than the total time. The implementation matches: urllib's socket timeout is per blocking operation, and both the direct TimeoutError (waiting for the response) and the URLError-wrapped timeout (connecting) are turned into FetchTimeout, so docs and code are consistent. tests/test_fetchlite.py uses only localhost sockets (an http.server and a listening socket that never replies), with an autouse fixture setting no_proxy so a runner proxy cannot interfere. The installer's default brownfield state (no cycle) is left untouched; Navigator needs no workflow records.
